One enduring feature of both regimes was the ability to harness charisma and propaganda to create a compelling narrative about national destiny. Hitler’s regime embodied a cult of personality that fused mythic symbolism, pseudo-scientific racism, and mass spectacle to forge a sense of unity and purpose. Stalin’s leadership relied on a parallel dramaturgy—triumphant declarations, carefully choreographed public appearances, and a narrative of relentless progress under the banner of socialist modernization. The regime’s legal system, police, and gatekeeping institutions were reorganized to eliminate political rivals, target ethnic and political others, and normalize a regime of terror. In Nazi Germany, rapid militarization, autarkic economic ambitions, and the expansionist logic of Lebensraum were framed as restoring national dignity and strength after perceived humiliation. In the Soviet Union, aggressive industrialization, agricultural collectivization, and the rhetoric of building a socialist future were presented as the path to societal fulfillment. Second, the consolidation of power should be constrained by the rule of law, an independent judiciary, and protections for civil liberties, because centralized power is inherently prone to abuse when not continually subjected to external constraints.
